benchmark_type_evidence: We collectively refer to this benchmark as IndicGLUE and it is a collection of (i) existing Indian language datasets for some tasks, (ii) manual translations of some English datasets into Indian languages done as a part of this work, and (iii) new datasets that were created semi-automatically for all major Indian languages as a part of this work.
brief_description: IndicNLPSuite provides monolingual corpora (IndicCorp), pre-trained word embeddings (IndicFT), language models (IndicBERT), and an NLU evaluation benchmark (IndicGLUE) for 11 major Indian languages from the Indo-Aryan and Dravidian families, comprising newly created semi-automatic datasets and curated existing datasets across tasks including text classification, QA, NER, NLI, paraphrase detection, and sentiment analysis.

all_annotators_native_speakers.evidence: For WNLI and COPA translations: 'skilled bilingual speakers' were used, verified by expert. The four new IndicGLUE datasets are semi-automatically generated (no human annotation). For external datasets, annotator details are not described in this paper.

annotator_workforce.compensation_details: For WNLI and COPA translations: 'The annotators were paid 3 cents per word.'
annotator_workforce.evidence: The paper describes authors from IIT Madras, AI4Bharat, and Microsoft India. For translated datasets (WNLI, COPA), skilled bilingual speakers were hired at 3 cents per word. The four new IndicGLUE datasets were created semi-automatically. No IRB/ethics review mentioned.

cultural_flags.english_centricity_notes: Two datasets (WNLI, COPA) are direct translations from English benchmarks, inheriting English-centric content. WikiAnn NER propagates English entity labels via cross-lingual links. The cross-lingual sentence retrieval task uses English as the source language. However, the majority of IndicGLUE datasets (4 new + 8 existing) are natively authored in Indian languages. The paper deliberately excluded Wikipedia from pretraining data to avoid overlap with evaluation datasets.

notably_excluded: Indo-Aryan languages beyond the 7 covered (e.g., Nepali, Sindhi, Kashmiri)
geographic_representation.evidence: The paper covers 11 major Indian languages from two families: Indo-Aryan (Punjabi, Hindi, Bengali, Odia, Assamese, Gujarati, Marathi) and Dravidian (Kannada, Telugu, Malayalam, Tamil). The paper notes 'The Indo-Aryan and Dravidian languages are spoken by 96% of the population in India. The other families are diverse, but the speaker population is relatively small.'
